slides.title: Chapter 24: Text-to-Speech and Speech Recognition Engines
slides.say: Chapter 23 taught a program to act on the screen. Chapter 24 teaches a program to speak and to listen: pyttsx3 turns text into speech, Whisper turns speech into text, the writers of whisper.utils turn the text into subtitle files, and yt-dlp downloads the audio of a video. The chapter has 17 listings and 1 table, and ends with 7 practice questions and 3 practice programs. This deck follows the chapter in its own order: the engine and its settings, saving speech as a WAV file, the Whisper models and what they hear, the subtitle files, the downloader, and the three practice programs, and it adds what the research found when the chapter's 46 printed statements were replayed. Nothing in the deck is heard. The machine has no sound card, so the console above shows that /dev/snd does not exist, and every program writes its speech to a WAV file that it deletes afterwards. Every output on the slides was printed by Python 3.14.6 with pyttsx3 2.99, openai-whisper 20250625, yt-dlp 2026.8.19 and NumPy 2.5.4, the versions the console above prints, with eSpeak NG 1.51 and ffmpeg 6.1.1 on the path. Windows, macOS, a microphone, a GPU, a cloud key and any download from YouTube were never used. What could not be run is marked NOT EXECUTED on its slide, and what the research measured and this deck does not run again is marked Recorded. Every count and time from one run is a single run on a machine with two cores, and not a benchmark.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: The route has six parts. It starts with what a script can do: the seven uses of the engines, the packages and tools they need, and the pinned release of pyttsx3 against the newest. Then speaking text: say() only queues, the voices, the rate and the volume, the WAV file, and the calls that never return. The third part is recognising speech: the Whisper models and Table 24-1, transcribing a sentence, ffmpeg, and the languages Whisper hears. The fourth is subtitles and downloading: the SRT, VTT and TSV files, the writer options and the time grid, the metadata of a video and the download of its audio. The fifth is practice and the replay: the guessing game that speaks, the 99 bottles of beer, the transcriber loop, and the chapter replayed in four environments. The last part is a one-map summary and the resources. The ranges name the exact slides, so you can return to the part you need. Four of the six stories are on slides and two are told in the notes, each with a link; the seven narrative diagrams of the chapter are drawn from the same specifications as the interactive page. Every output was printed by Python 3.14.6 with pyttsx3 2.99, openai-whisper 20250625 and yt-dlp 2026.8.19, nothing is heard, and what could not be run is marked on its slide.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: The first question is the spine of the chapter, and the deck answers it slide by slide. On a machine with no sound card, no microphone and no GPU, a program can still list the voices of the engine, change the rate and the volume, save speech as a WAV file, transcribe that file with Whisper, write subtitle files and ask yt-dlp for the metadata of a video, and every one of those can be checked because the result is a file or a number. What cannot be shown to work is the part that needs a person or a service: the sound itself, a microphone, a GPU, Windows and macOS, the cloud services, and any download from YouTube, whose Terms of Service do not allow it. The second question is the watch-out. The chapter's 17 listings hold 45 statements, 46 with the one that was substituted, and the research replayed them as printed. With Python 3.14.6 and the newest packages 34 of the 46 matched the book's output, 42 ran without an exception, 1 raised and 3 were not executed; the pinned set gave 35, 42, 1 and 3, the empty environment 8, 8, 35 and 3, and the set without ffmpeg 32, 38, 5 and 3. The statements that differ are the Voice objects and names, the line Audio saved to that the driver prints, the transcription of hello.wav, the TSV listing and the call of speak(), which no listing defines. Each slide says where a printed line differs and on what evidence. The spread between releases is large too: of the 22 releases of pyttsx3, 8 ran and 9 crashed with a segmentation fault, and Appendix A pins a pyttsx3 that saves a truncated file.

slides.title: What a script can do with the engines
slides.say: Wikipedia's article on speech synthesis says that Homer Dudley developed, after his work on the vocoder, a keyboard-operated voice synthesizer called the Voder (Voice Demonstrator), which he exhibited at the 1939 New York World's Fair. A person played it with keys; nothing in it read text. In this study pyttsx3 2.99 with eSpeak NG 1.51 listed 131 voices, each a Voice object with a name, a gender, an age and a list of languages, and all 131 said Male with the age None, so a voice is a language and a set of rules, not a person. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Speech synthesis' (Homer Dudley, the Voder, the 1939 New York World's Fair), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves VoiceObjects and PersistentVoice. The use-case diagram lists what a script can do with the engines of the chapter: list the voices of the engine, change the rate of the speech, save speech as a WAV file, transcribe audio with transcribe(), write a subtitle file, read the metadata of a video and download audio with download(). They are independent calls into three libraries, which is why the picture is a set of uses and not a sequence. The console runs under the interpreter of the deck. ffmpeg and espeak-ng are on the path, /dev/snd does not exist, audioop is gone from this Python and wave is not: PEP 594 removed audioop, aifc, sunau, chunk and sndhdr in Python 3.13, and the wave module that pyttsx3 uses stayed. The card records what the research found on 14 October 2026 and this deck does not run again: the chapter page returned 200 with 44,667 bytes and its sha256 equals the digest in the book's own chapter ontology; the online materials are a zip of 91 files, 72 of them Python, and none of them imports whisper or yt_dlp or holds hello.wav, audio.srt or metadata.json. The publisher's book page names the chapter once and Whisper, pyttsx3 and yt-dlp not at all.

slides.title: Packages and the tools they need
slides.say: Wikipedia's article on eSpeak says that in 1995 Jonathan Duddington released the Speak speech synthesizer for RISC OS computers supporting British English, and that on 17 February 2006 Speak 1.05 was released under the GPLv2 license, initially for Linux. Development continued until it was renamed eSpeak, and eSpeak NG continues it. In this study pyttsx3 2.99 started with eSpeak NG 1.51 and saved a WAV, but with only the package the chapter names (espeak 1.48.15) its init raised ValueError for the voice gmw/en, and with neither it raised RuntimeError. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'ESpeak' (Speak of 1995 for RISC OS, Speak 1.05 under the GPLv2 on 17 February 2006), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves EspeakDependency and LinuxEspeak. The table runs one probe in four interpreters while the deck is checked: Python 3.14.6 with the newest packages, Python 3.12.3 with the pinned pyttsx3 2.98 and openai-whisper 20231117 and NumPy 1.26.4, Python 3.14.6 with ffmpeg taken off the path, and an empty Python 3.14.6. The probe imports the packages, looks for ffmpeg and calls pyttsx3.init(); every row with the packages starts an Engine, the empty Python raises ModuleNotFoundError, and the row without ffmpeg shows the only difference that the probe can see. The chapter's Linux command installs espeak, the old package, and pyttsx3 2.99 needs espeak-ng: the research tried the four combinations on Ubuntu 24.04 and only the two that include espeak-ng started, with 131 voices, a saved WAV file and the library libespeak-ng.so.1. Appendix A pins the 2.98 release of pyttsx3, advises numpy below 2 and the CUDA 11.8 wheels of PyTorch, and says that the automateboringstuff3 package always installs the newest yt-dlp. It names neither ffmpeg nor espeak, and the next slides show what each one is needed for. SAPI5, NSSpeechSynthesizer, AVSpeech, the microphone, the GPU and the cloud services were read from their documentation and never run.

slides.title: The pinned release and the newest
slides.say: The sequence diagram is the story of the pin: the reader installs the pinned release of pyttsx3 from PyPI, PyPI delivers pyttsx3 2.98, the reader saves the sentence Hello. How are you doing?, and the engine truncates the file; with pyttsx3 2.99 the same sentence is saved whole. The program runs the same few lines in two interpreters, Python 3.12.3 with pyttsx3 2.98 and Python 3.14.6 with 2.99, and prints the length of the file each wrote: 0.6 and 0.51 seconds for the pinned release, 1.54 and 1.55 for the newest. The sentences are Hello. How are you doing? and One. Two. Three. The research found the cause in the driver: 2.98 writes the file at the first end-of-sentence event, before it adds the samples of that event, and it hands the file to ffmpeg, so a name ending in .mp3 gave a real MP3 file, .ogg a real Ogg file, and with no ffmpeg on the path no file at all, while 2.99 writes a WAV file through the wave module whatever the extension says. The table is the research's record of the releases it tried: of 22 releases of pyttsx3, 8 ran on Python 3.14.6, 9 (2.71 to 2.95) crashed with a segmentation fault and 5 needed macOS; of 13 releases of openai-whisper, 6 ran on Python 3.12.3, 1 had an import error and 6, 20230307 to 20231106, could not be installed there because they require triton 2.0.0; of the 6 last stable yt-dlp releases of 2021 to 2026, 5 ran and 2021.12.27 stopped on the missing imghdr module that Python 3.13 removed. Pinning is not safe by itself: the pinned openai-whisper also needed setuptools below 81 and no build isolation before it would install.

slides.title: say() only queues the text
slides.say: The life of an utterance has three states. The text is in the queue after say(); the utterance has started when runAndWait() fires started-utterance; and it has finished when the engine fires finished-utterance. The program connects both events to a list and shows the three moments. say() returns None at once, no event has fired and isBusy() already reports True, because the text is only in the queue. After setProperty('rate', 300) the rate still reads 200, since a property is applied when runAndWait() processes the queue, and it reads 300 after the call. The events list ends with started-utterance and finished-utterance, in that order. say('') does not raise an error: it returns the text Argument value can't be None or empty. The research also saw that save_to_file('') raised AssertionError, and that with no sound card, which is the case here, runAndWait() returned with exit code 0 although aplay printed an audio open error, so a program that speaks to nobody does not fail. The program of the slide never plays a sound: the engine is asked to speak, the audio device is absent and nothing is heard, which is the local stand-in the slide names.

slides.title: The voices of the engine
slides.say: The program lists the voices of eSpeak NG through pyttsx3 2.99: 131 Voice objects, the first of them Afrikaans with the gender Male, the age None and the languages ['af']. All 131 say Male, none has an age, and 8 are English. The voice the engine starts with is gmw/en. The chapter's listing 4 prints the names of Windows voices, David and Zira; no voice here has those names, and the research confirmed that none of the 131 names contains them. The chapter then sets the voice to voices[1].id, which on this engine is sem/am, Amharic, so the program speaks the same sentence with it and saves hello.wav. The research measured 0.89 seconds for that file and 1.54 seconds for the default voice; this deck's own run of the program prints 1.48 seconds for voices[1], and the difference is one more reason to treat a time as a single run. A Voice object is not a string: printing a list of voices shows addresses, one of the statements of the chapter that cannot match its book. SAPI5 and NSSpeechSynthesizer, the drivers of Windows and macOS, were read from their sources and documentation, and were not executed.

slides.title: Rate and volume
slides.say: The chart is the length in seconds of the same ten-word sentence, The quick brown fox jumps over the yellow lazy dog, at seven rates, each set in a fresh process: 6.46 seconds at rate 50, 5.44 at 100, 3.62 at 150, 2.70 at 200, which is the default, 2.16 at 250, 1.76 at 300 and 1.26 at 400. The rate is the speed in words per minute that the engine is asked for, and the measured speed at the default is about 222 words per minute. The volume is a number from 0 to 1 that scales the samples: the largest sample is 26394 at volume 1.0, 19622 at 0.75, 13024 at 0.5, 2222 at 0.1 and 0 at 0.0, and volume 5 gives 32768, the end of what 16 bits hold, so the sound is clipped and the chapter's advice to keep the volume at or below 1 is not a matter of taste. The picture shows the two files at a common time scale: the slow one, rate 100, is longer than the fast one, rate 300. Each value comes from a separate process because the rate set with setProperty() is only applied when runAndWait() runs, as the previous slide showed. The research set the rate before each of seven files in one process and got the same seven lengths in its run. All of these are single runs.

slides.title: Saving speech as a WAV file
slides.say: save_to_file() does not write anything when it is called: the program prints that hello.wav does not exist before runAndWait(), and the file appears when the queue is processed. The file for Hello. How are you doing? has 1 channel, 2 bytes per sample, a rate of 22,050 Hz and 33,948 frames, which is 1.54 seconds and 67,940 bytes, and it is written with the wave module. The chapter says the file can have another extension; pyttsx3 2.99 writes a WAV whatever the name says, so the file hello.mp3 begins with RIFF and WAVE, and the research found that ffprobe called it a wav file. The pinned 2.98, by contrast, handed the file to ffmpeg. The picture is the waveform of hello.wav, saved by the same program: the greater the amplitude the taller the strip, and the pauses between the words are the flat parts. Because the file can be incomplete when runAndWait() returns, the program calls a small helper that waits until the size of the file has not changed for a moment; the next slide shows why. In the research 1,800 words of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland became 450.2 seconds, 7.5 minutes, of audio in about 3 seconds of work, where the chapter says 10 minutes in about 2 seconds; that is one run on this machine.

slides.title: A call that never returns
slides.say: The activity diagram is the safe way to save a sentence: initialise the engine, call save_to_file() with the text and the file name, call runAndWait() to process the queue, and then ask whether the file is complete; if it is, open it with the wave module, and if not, wait until the size of the file is stable and ask again. The program shows the two ways a call does not come back, each in a child process that is given 5 seconds. A runAndWait() with nothing to say, after a property was changed, returns the first time and does not return the second time; and a save_to_file() into a folder that does not exist returns as the first call of a process and does not return after an utterance. The research killed both after 15 seconds. It also found that the file is not always complete when the first runAndWait() returns: in 12 fresh processes that was so in 8 for a text of 33 words and in none for a text of 5 words. A program that opens the file straight away may read half of it, which is why the helper waits for the size to settle. The hanging calls are written here as a warning, and the safest habit is one runAndWait() after all the calls, and a folder that exists.

slides.title: The Whisper models
slides.say: Table 24-1 of the chapter lists five models with a file size, the time to transcribe 10 words and the time for 15 minutes: tiny 74MB, 1.9 s and 1m 20s; base 142MB, 3.0 s and 2m 34s; small 472MB, 9.6 s and 6m 37s; medium 1.5GB, 28.6 s and 20m 17s; large-v3 3GB, 51.9 s and 32m 58s. The table of the slide sets the book beside this machine. The files have 75,572,083 bytes for tiny, 145,262,807 for base, 483,617,219 for small and 3,087,371,615 for large-v3, so the book's sizes are rounded down; the program counts the parameters of the three models that load, 37.2, 71.8 and 240.6 million, and reads the sizes of their files. On two CPU cores the research measured 1.0, 1.6 and 5.1 seconds for the ten words where the table says 1.9, 3.0 and 9.6, and the memory of the process peaked at 972, 1,082 and 2,645 MiB. These are single runs on one machine, not the author's laptop. Loading medium and turbo ended with the kernel's out-of-memory killer, return code -9, on a machine with 8,029 MiB of memory; the README of Whisper lists about 6 GB for turbo and about 10 GB for large. large-v3 could not be loaded under a 6.5 GB address-space limit. These are findings, not successes. The package knows 14 model names, turbo among them. The program asks for device='cuda' and gets RuntimeError, because torch.cuda.is_available() is False; no GPU was used for anything in this deck.

slides.title: Transcribing a sentence
slides.say: Wikipedia's article on Whisper says it was created by OpenAI and first released as open-source software in September 2022, and that its training dataset consists of 680,000 hours of labeled audio-transcript pairs sourced from the internet, including 117,000 hours in 96 non-English languages. The weights are files that the package downloads on first use. In this study the file of the tiny model had 75,572,083 bytes and that of the base model 145,262,807 bytes, where the chapter's table says 74MB and 142MB, and the large-v3 file had 3,087,371,615 bytes. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Whisper (speech recognition system)' (released in September 2022; 680,000 hours; 117,000 hours in 96 non-English languages), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves ModelFiles and WhisperPackage. The program speaks the ten-word sentence of the chapter, The quick brown fox jumps over the yellow lazy dog, into fox.wav and transcribes the file with the three models. tiny hears the quick brown fog stump over the yellow laser dog, base the quick round fox dumps over the yellow lazy dog, and small the quick brown fox dumps over the yellow lazy dog. The word error rate, the number of words to change divided by the number of words said, is 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1, which the chart draws. The result is a dictionary with the keys text, segments and language, and each segment has the keys id, seek, start, end, text and tokens. The default of transcribe() may retry with a random temperature, which is why the programs of this deck pass temperature=0.0 wherever the text is printed: the same file gives the same text twice. A word error rate of one sentence is only a count. The research measured 0.1919, 0.1079 and 0.0345 on the 1,800 words read by eSpeak NG, between 0.1636 and 0.3123 for tiny, 0.1524 and 0.2565 for base and 0.0186 and 0.2416 for small on four LibriVox readings of the Gettysburg Address, and it saw tiny transcribe ten seconds of digital silence as the word You. Speech made by a synthesiser is easy and a human voice is not; a transcript is the text of a model and not a copy of what was said.

slides.title: Whisper needs ffmpeg
slides.say: The flow chart is the first half of every transcription: load a model, ask whether ffmpeg is on the path, and, if it is, call transcribe() and then get_writer() to write the subtitle file; if it is not, the call raises FileNotFoundError and the chain ends. The chapter names ffmpeg only inside a comment of the yt-dlp listing, and Appendix A never names it, yet whisper.load_audio() starts ffmpeg for every file. With it on the path a WAV file becomes a float32 array of 43,129 samples at 16,000 Hz, the rate Whisper wants whatever the rate of the file was. The program empties the path for two calls and both raise FileNotFoundError: load_audio() itself and transcribe(), which calls it. The picture is the signal after the conversion, the same speech at 16 kHz. The research found the same for yt-dlp: without ffmpeg, extracting audio raised DownloadError, ffprobe and ffmpeg not found, and left downloaded_content.mp3 instead of the m4a that listing 13 looks for, so a missing tool shows up far from where it is needed. The package manager of the system, not pip, installs ffmpeg, which is why the probe of slide 5 looks for it.

slides.title: Languages and what Whisper hears
slides.say: Wikipedia's article on speech recognition says that in 1952 Bell Labs researchers Stephen Balashek, R. Biddulph and K. H. Davis built Audrey for single-speaker digit recognition, and that the system located the formants in the power spectrum of each utterance. It knew one speaker and the ten digits. In this study Whisper tiny named the language of the same eSpeak sentence correctly for 3 of 6 languages and base for 4 of 6, and heard the ten-word fox sentence with a word error rate of 0.3 (tiny), 0.2 (base) and 0.1 (small). The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Speech recognition' (Audrey, 1952; Balashek, Biddulph and Davis), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves LanguagesAndDetection and ModelWerTable. The program speaks one sentence in each of six languages with the voices of eSpeak NG, Turkish, German, French, Spanish, Italian and English, and asks tiny and base which language they hear. tiny named the language right for 3 of the 6 and base for 4: the Turkish sentence was heard as Thai by both, German as Danish by tiny, and Italian as Korean by tiny and as Spanish by base; the research, which used a Chinese sentence where this deck uses Italian, got the same totals, 3 and 4. Whisper 20250625 knows 100 languages, and asking for a language it does not know, here klingon, raises ValueError, Unsupported language. A transcript is a model's text: tiny and base wrote Hello, how are you doing for the sentence the book prints as Hello. How are you doing?, so a program that compares a transcript with the text it spoke has to normalise case and punctuation first, as the word error rate of the previous slide does. The synthesised speech is clean and unnatural, and the numbers say nothing about a human voice, an accent or noise.

slides.title: Subtitle files: SRT, VTT and TSV
slides.say: Wikipedia's article on SubRip says the program, developed by Brain and Zuggy for Microsoft Windows, was released on 3 March 2000, and that the SubRip Text file format has the filename extension .srt and the internet media type application/x-subrip. Its blocks are a number, a time range and text. In this study Whisper's SRT writer produced the chapter's 223-byte listing exactly for the two segments the book prints, wrote times with a comma before the milliseconds (01:00:01,500), and its WebVTT writer used a full stop (01:00:01.500). The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'SubRip' (Brain and Zuggy, released 3 March 2000, the extension .srt), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves SrtListing and ReadBackCues. The program gives the writers of whisper.utils the two segments the chapter prints, a first cue from 0.0 to 5.64 seconds and a second from 5.64 to 14.96, and writes them in three formats. The SRT file has 223 bytes, the WebVTT file 215 and the TSV file 190, and the SRT and VTT files equal the chapter's listings 7 and 8, the research found them equal under the pinned release too. They differ in the shape of the time: SRT counts hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds with a comma, 00:00:05,640, WebVTT drops the hours and uses a point, 00:05.640, and the TSV file has the columns start, end and text, separated by tabs and counted in milliseconds, where the chapter's listing 9 shows spaces. get_writer() accepts srt, vtt, tsv, txt and json; asking for docx raises KeyError. The picture draws the two cues on a time axis, one bar for each. The W3C specification of WebVTT and the SubRip format are in the resources.

slides.title: Writer options and the time grid
slides.say: The program transcribes the Gettysburg Address, a public-domain LibriVox reading hosted by the Internet Archive, with tiny: 26 segments, written as 26 SRT blocks, and 52 times, a start and an end for each segment. Of the 52, all 52 are multiples of 0.02 seconds, which is the resolution of Whisper's timestamps and the reason a subtitle time never shows a finer step. With word_timestamps=True the first segment holds 14 words with a time each, and with the writer options max_line_width=30 and max_line_count=2 the same text is cut into 31 blocks with lines of at most 30 characters; the first block shows how a long cue is wrapped. The options are keyword arguments of the writer, not of transcribe(), and the word-level times are only produced when transcribe() was asked for them. The archive.org file stands in for YouTube: the deck never used YouTube, and the file is checked against its SHA-256 before use.

slides.title: yt-dlp: the metadata of a video
slides.say: extract_info(url, download=False) returns a dictionary and downloads nothing. The program asks for the metadata of the Gettysburg reading on archive.org, which stands in for YouTube: 53 keys, 3 formats, the extractor archive.org and the title The Gettysburg Address. Of the 13 keys the chapter prints, id, title, formats, thumbnails, description, duration and webpage_url are here and 6 are missing: thumbnail, channel_id, channel_url, view_count, average_rating and age_limit belong to a video site. The prose of the chapter says that YoutubeDL has a sanitize() method; it has sanitize_info() and no sanitize, and the program shows both attributes. sanitize_info() makes the dictionary JSON-serializable, as the yt-dlp README says, and writing the result gives a metadata.json of 55 keys. For the chapter's own video, Beyond the Basic Stuff with Python by Al Sweigart, the research recorded 76 keys, 16 formats and 565 seconds; on the same day one request failed with a request to sign in to confirm you're not a bot and a later one succeeded, so a result from YouTube is not repeatable.

slides.title: Downloading audio
slides.say: The chapter downloads the audio of a YouTube video. This deck cannot do that for a reason that is not technical: the Terms of Service of YouTube do not allow downloading any part of the service or its content except as expressly authorized, so the study downloaded a public-domain LibriVox reading from the Internet Archive instead, and this deck does the same. download() returned 0 and left downloaded_content.m4a, an AAC stream of 100.3 seconds, converted by ffmpeg from a 64 kbit/s mp3 of 100.4 seconds. A string in place of a list was accepted, as the research found, which is a leniency and not a promise; an address that is nowhere raised DownloadError with HTTP Error 404. The options dictionary names the output template, the format and a postprocessor that extracts the audio as m4a, so the conversion needs ffmpeg, the tool of slide 14. The YouTube download itself, and every other site the supported-sites list names, was NOT EXECUTED, and the research recorded what happens without ffmpeg.

slides.title: A guessing game that speaks
slides.say: The first practice program of the chapter asks for a guessing game that speaks. The chapter's listing 16 calls speak(), which no listing defines, and it raised NameError in every environment the research tried, so the program of the slide defines its own. The idea is to pass the engine into the game. make_speak() builds a speak() that prints the text and then says it, and game() takes speak as a parameter, so a test can pass a Recorder, a stand-in engine that only keeps the lines, and the real game can pass a Writer, an engine whose say() saves each line to a WAV file. With the Recorder the game said 4 lines in 3 guesses and the second line was 10 is too low; with the Writer the same 4 lines were written to line1.wav to line4.wav. The lengths of the four files depend on the text: with the longer sentences of the research they were 2.56, 1.94, 1.95 and 2.5 seconds, and the shorter sentences of this program give the lengths the transcript prints. Nothing is spoken aloud, and the point of the exercise is that a program which takes its engine as an argument can be tested without a loudspeaker.

slides.title: 99 bottles of beer
slides.say: Wikipedia's article on Daisy Bell says that in 1961 an IBM 7090 at Bell Labs was programmed to sing the song, one of the earliest demonstrations of computer speech synthesis. Arthur C. Clarke saw a demonstration at Bell Labs in 1962 and referred to it in the 1968 novel and film 2001: A Space Odyssey, in which the HAL 9000 computer sings it during its gradual deactivation. In this study the chapter's song program for 99 bottles of beer made 396 lines and 2,377 words, and pyttsx3 wrote them as 699.3 seconds of audio in 7.5 seconds of work, without a note of music. The account rests on these sources. Wikipedia, 'Daisy Bell' (the IBM 7090 of 1961, Clarke in 1962, HAL 9000), read 2026-10-14; this study's leaves SongLyrics and SongAudio. The second practice program asks for the song of 99 bottles of beer, sung by the engine. bottles() and verse() write the verse for a number, with 1 bottle in the singular and No more bottles at the end, and the program prints the verses for 2 and for 1. The whole song is 99 verses, 396 lines, 2,377 words and 11,457 characters. The engine writes the first 3 verses as 18.3 seconds of audio and the 99 verses as 699.3 seconds, 11.7 minutes, and 30.8 MB of WAV; in the research the same 99 verses took 7.5 seconds of work. The picture is the waveform of the 3-verse file. The research also asked tiny to transcribe the 3 verses and got a word error rate of 0.9589, nearly every word wrong. The sentence of the chapter, that the program takes a long time, is true of the audio and not of the work: the audio is 11.7 minutes long and it is made in seconds. All of these are single runs.

slides.title: The transcriber loop
slides.say: The third practice program asks for a function that takes a list of addresses, downloads the audio of each, transcribes it and writes subtitle files. The sequence diagram is that loop: the script calls download() with the address, yt-dlp returns the audio file, the script calls transcribe() on it, Whisper returns the result, and the writers write an SRT, a VTT and a TXT file. The program runs it on two public-domain LibriVox readings of the Gettysburg Address on archive.org, which stand in for YouTube: the first gave 26 segments and 312 words, the second 17 segments and 304 words, and each left an m4a, an SRT, a VTT and a TXT file. The research timed the loop at 47.8 seconds for the two readings. The last lines pass an address that is nowhere: the function raises DownloadError, and since nothing in the loop catches it, one bad address stops the whole list. A version that caught the error and went on to the next address is the obvious improvement. The options dictionary of slide 19 is held in a helper here so that the function fits the slide, and the hidden lines say so.

slides.title: The chapter replayed in four environments
slides.say: The table is the research's record of the chapter's statements replayed as printed, and the deck check computes every cell again from the record. With Python 3.14.6 and the newest packages 34 of the 46 matched the book and 42 ran without an exception; the pinned set, Python 3.12.3 with pyttsx3 2.98 and openai-whisper 20231117, gave 35 and 42; in the empty environment 8 matched and 8 ran; without ffmpeg 32 matched and 38 ran. The statements that differ are the Voice objects and names, the line Audio saved to that the driver prints, the transcription of hello.wav, the TSV listing and the call of speak. One program that saves speech, lists voices and asks yt-dlp questions ran under 11 interpreters, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14.0 to 3.14.6 and 3.15.0b4, and compared 14 items. Only 2 differed, both about aifc, audioop, sunau, chunk and sndhdr, which import under 3.11 and 3.12 and fail from 3.13, while wave, which pyttsx3 uses, stayed; the Whisper version compared 16 items and 2 differed, only in the printed form of a type. Appendix B of the book gives 7 answers for the chapter. The research confirmed that pyttsx3 and Whisper need no internet once the tiny model is on disk, and found that answer 5 is wrong about the default model: load_model has no default for the name, and the whisper command defaults to turbo in 20250625 and to small in 20231117. The photograph of the stories was not fetched, because the request to Wikimedia answered 429.

slides.title: The chapter in one map
slides.say: These six branches are the route of the deck. The text-to-speech engine: pyttsx3 queues text with say(), runAndWait() processes the queue, and the rate and the volume are properties; on slide 7 the rate still read 200 after it was set to 300 until runAndWait() had run. Saved speech and recognition: save_to_file() writes a WAV file, Whisper needs ffmpeg, and the models differ in size and time; slide 12 sets the book's table beside this machine. Subtitle files: the writers make SRT, VTT and TSV files, the times are on a grid of 0.02 seconds, and the word error rate measures accuracy. Downloading videos: yt-dlp downloads audio, the terms of the site limit downloading, and downloaders change with the releases, so 5 of 6 recent yt-dlp releases ran. Practice programs: the guessing game speaks, the song has 99 verses, and the transcriber loop stops at a bad address. Environment and evidence: the study ran Python 3.14.6, Windows and macOS were not executed, and every number is from a single run. Together they answer the first question of the chapter, what can be shown to work without a sound card, a microphone or a GPU and what can only be shown to fail, and the slides that say where a printed line differs answer the second. The map is drawn from the same specification as the interactive page.

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Every link on this slide was opened on the day the deck was made, and the build records the status each answered. The textbook chapter is free to read online and holds every listing of the chapter; the online materials are the zip of 91 files, and Appendix A is where the book installs third-party packages. The reference links are the PyPI page of pyttsx3, the README of Whisper, the README of yt-dlp with its section on embedding the downloader in Python, the specification of WebVTT and the documentation of the wave module. The six stories of the chapter have their own link, and their pages are the first group. The research package holds 69 sources in all, among them the source of the eSpeak driver of pyttsx3, the PyPI metadata of the three packages, the paper Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision, the supported-sites list of yt-dlp and the Terms of Service of YouTube. The book recommends Make Python Talk by Liu for more on speech. No photograph of a person is used in the deck.

slides.title: What you should now be able to say
slides.say: Four claims, each carried by a result you saw printed. If you can say them in your own words and run the examples yourself, you have the chapter. The programs need pyttsx3, openai-whisper and yt-dlp, with eSpeak NG and ffmpeg installed by the package manager of the system, and a work folder they can fill with WAV files. The rows were run again under Python 3.14.6 each time the deck was built, and the programs, and with them the pictures, were run again by the check that compares the slides with the recording. What was not run is marked on its slide: SAPI5, NSSpeechSynthesizer and AVSpeech, a microphone, a GPU, the cloud services, a download from YouTube, and the Whisper models medium, turbo and large-v3. Nothing was ever heard. Every count and time in this deck from a single run is a single run, and not a benchmark. The next chapter of the book moves on, and what this chapter taught about checking what a program writes carries over.
